nameStory: This little spring wildflower gets its name from the small underground bulb that stores energy through winter, making it 'bulbous.' The 'cress' part comes from an old word meaning 'to grow' or 'increase,' referring to how these plants spread in wet areas. Early settlers called many peppery mustard family plants 'cress' because they tasted similar to watercress.
description: Bulbous cress is a small perennial wildflower that pops up in wet woodlands each spring. It grows about 6-12 inches tall with a cluster of white, four-petaled flowers that seem to float above the leaves like tiny stars. The plant has a mix of rounded basal leaves near the ground and more angular stem leaves that climb upward. It's one of those charming spring ephemerals that brightens up soggy forest floors before the trees fully leaf out.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright white flowers with exactly four petals arranged in a cross shape, clustered at the top of the stem well above the foliage in late spring

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two types of leaves: rounded, kidney-shaped leaves at the base and more angular, toothed leaves along the stem that feel smooth and slightly succulent

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant reaching 6-12 inches tall, often forming small colonies in wet spots with flowers held noticeably above the leafy base

idTips.label: Taste
idTips.description: Leaves have a distinct peppery, watercress-like bite when chewed - sharp and tangy like horseradish but milder

idTips.label: Root
idTips.description: Small underground bulb or tuber that can be felt if you gently probe the soil around the base of the plant

habitat: Look for bulbous cress in the moist, rich soils of bottomland forests, swamps, and wet woodland edges throughout New England. It particularly loves areas with limestone or other calcium-rich soils, often growing alongside skunk cabbage, marsh marigold, and wild ginger. You'll spot it in those soggy spots where spring water seeps through the forest floor.

seasonality.spring: This is prime time for bulbous cress! The distinctive white cross-shaped flowers bloom from April through May, standing tall above the fresh green foliage.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and the plant produces small seed pods. Leaves remain green and edible but become less noticeable as other vegetation grows up around it.
seasonality.fall: Above-ground parts begin to die back as the plant stores energy in its underground bulb for next year's growth.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground - all the plant's energy is stored in that small underground bulb waiting for spring.

funFact: This innocent-looking wildflower is actually nature's horseradish! The peppery compounds in its leaves are chemically similar to those in horseradish and wasabi, and early settlers used bulbous cress as a spicy condiment on their meals.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small white spring wildflowers, but the four-petaled cross shape is your key clue - most other white spring flowers have five petals or different arrangements. The peppery taste is also a dead giveaway that you've found a mustard family member.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bittercress,' this plant isn't particularly bitter at all - it's actually quite pleasantly peppery. The 'bitter' in the name comes from an old botanical tradition of calling all Cardamine species bittercresses, even though their flavors vary considerably.
compareHints: Among its many Cardamine relatives in New England, bulbous cress stands out for its underground bulb and preference for very wet soils. Two-leaved toothwort has only two stem leaves and grows in drier woods, while hairy bittercress is much smaller and grows as a weedy annual in disturbed soils. The bulbous cress flowers are also held more prominently above the foliage than most of its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's toothworts and bittercresses, two-leaved toothwort is unique for its simple three-parted leaves and paired leaf arrangement.
Among New England's bittercresses, hairy bittercress is distinguished by its small size, annual habit, and compound leaves with rounded leaflets.

Among its bittercress relatives, narrow-leaved bittercress stands out for its particularly slender, lance-shaped leaflets—much narrower than the rounded leaflets of hairy bittercress or the broader segments of Pennsylvania bittercress.
Among New England's bittercresses, Pennsylvania bittercress stands out for its smooth leaves and taller stature.
Among New England's toothworts, cut-leaved stands out with its three deeply-divided leaves arranged in a whorl, while two-leaved toothwort has just two broader, less-divided leaves.
Among its Cardamine relatives in New England, cuckooflower stands out for preferring wetter habitats than most bittercresses and toothworts.
Among New England's bittercresses, nursery bittercress is distinguished by its completely smooth leaves and preference for disturbed garden soils.
Large toothwort differs from its close relative cut-leaved toothwort by having more finely divided, almost lacy leaflets and typically growing taller.
Among its bittercress relatives, sand bittercress is distinguished by its preference for sandy, dry soils and its particularly small size.

Alpine bittercress is dramatically different from its lowland Cardamine relatives in New England - while species like hairy bittercress and Pennsylvania bittercress are weedy annuals that pop up in gardens and disturbed areas, alpine bittercress is a specialized perennial that grows only in extreme mountain conditions.

Long's Bittercress differs from its relatives by having the most finely divided leaves in the genus - almost thread-like compared to the broader leaflets of Two-leaved Toothwort or the simpler leaves of Hairy Bittercress.

Among its Cardamine relatives in New England, Purple Cress is unique for its potential purple flower coloration - species like Two-leaved Toothwort and the various bittercresses typically stick to white or pale pink flowers.

Among the Cardamine genus in New England, white cuckoo bitter-cress has the most finely divided, feathery leaves - much more delicate than the broader leaflets of toothworts or the simpler leaves of other bitter-cresses.
Chinese Ivy differs from other Cardamine species in New England by being strictly aquatic and having a trailing, mat-forming growth habit.
